utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, assisted this morning by Timothy Resch, who will be calling tomorrow's witness, who is also going to be a witness in another trial in which Mr. Resch is engaged. And he's here this morning to see how Your Honours operate and also as usual, Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. David Cunningham with Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Any preliminaries, yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, only one thing. Your Honour asked on Friday for a chart, as it were, of the documents that came from AID, which this witness is able to authenticate. That will be available after the first break for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I realised also, Ms. Korner, after I asked you, I mean, it was a lapse of memory for -- which is not usual with me, but I did realise after all that I had already in my possession this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it was not complete. In other words, it does give me an indication of the provenance of many of the documents that have been made use of by this witness, but not all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, we -- I know there were ones where originally Mr. Inayat could not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But we changed that because we were able to obtain the same documents from a traceable source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we can provide Your Honours with an updated one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's better, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we're going to do is we've done two things in this trial. The first is that we've identified the documents which this witness has authenticated. Equally, we've identified the documents that Mr. Hidic also himself had copies of so that they came -- the identical documents but which came from a separate source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Hidic testify in open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Your Honour, there are two -- the chart will have two columns. Now, Your Honour, the only other things, I have to ask Your Honours this. Clearly, because of time constraints, I have not taken him through every document that he could authenticate. There are lots more that come from AID but which I haven't shown him. Your Honour, if I do that, if Your Honours feel it important enough, that's going to take up more time. So Your Honour, I'm hoping that Your Honours will regard his evidence on some as strong enough to draw an inference on the others. Otherwise, I will have to take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't expect me or my colleagues to comment on that. We're definitely not going to tell you whether we are prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will be overstepping the limits.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I don't think you are. I think there must come a stage where these objections which are just delivered, because they happen to come from AID, either the Defence properly withdraw them, which they ought, because this is just a waste of Court time, or alternatively, I think Your Honours are entitled to say where Court time comes into consideration and where there is no real foundation for anything that's been suggested about those documents, other than they came from AID, that Your Honours ought to be able to say, in our respectful submission, to the Defence, enough is enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is another solution, Ms. Korner. I don't know how much more questions you have left. I think the gist of the witness's -- or the substance of his testimony is already there. Perhaps you could stop here with questioning, tender his statement or his interview in evidence, we'll suspend the sitting for -- I don't know, half an hour or whatever, you give him all the documents that you require him to authenticate, and we'll reconvene when he has finished going through them, and he will just confirm authentication, or not confirm. I mean, I don't know. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the other thing I can do, Your Honour, I can certainly tender the rest of the interview. He needs to explain a couple more entries in his diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's understandable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other thing is I read over the weekend the statement of the next witness, BT93.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Originally it was scheduled to -- for two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't -- I think we don't even require a day to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think he'll take two days either, which is why I've indicated to Mr. Cunningham if this witness goes a little longer then of course he can go into tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which basically means this: If you agree with me, and if Mr. Cunningham agrees with me that we can finish that witness -- I don't know, Wednesday or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness who is following would certainly finish by Wednesday. We hope in time to do a little bit of what we call in general, I think, housekeeping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm flexible. See what you prefer, and I think we will accommodate you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we see how we go, then, and if necessary, what I will do is ask the witness to remain when he's completed his evidence and make -- just go through all the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. What I certainly -- I mean, I'm just making myself clear. What I certainly do not intend to do is to deprive Mr. Cunningham from even one minute of cross-examination if he thinks he needs it with this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm making myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's bring the witness in. Still in open session now, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, will you be taking the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will. All right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I don't think it's a two-day witness either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I think it's -- anyway. Unless he's got things to say which are not in his statement, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, usher. Good morning to you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you had a nice weekend and that you recharged your batteries and are ready for your final day in the Tribunal, let's hope.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please make the declaration and we can start again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a chair. Yes, Ms. Korner. Examined by Ms. Korner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge. Could you have your diary back for a moment, or for more than a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if Your Honours would like to go, please, to the 2nd of July entry. I dealt with the document for the 2nd of July, that is, the actual minutes of the Crisis Staff meeting, on Friday. And I'll just tell Your Honours what the number was. It was, in fact, P1841. But I want to ask a couple of questions about your diary entry. It's page 122 of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you say 2nd of June or 2nd of July? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2nd of July, please. Are these your notes of the -- of what was said to happen at the Crisis Staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are my notes, except that I'm wondering the way the order in which this is put, it could have been the 1st of July. But yes, they are the notes. It was the 42nd meeting, if that is what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I want to ask you about a couple of things, please, in your notes. We see, and does it have a tick next to it, to call Pero Dosen, "sorting out relations, plan definite"? Now, can you just tell the Court who Pero Dosen was?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pero Dosen was a chief in Radio Petrovac. That is Pero Dosen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you now tell us what "sorting out relations, plan definite" referred to? If you can't remember, say so straight away.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite remember, but it could have been the matter of funding the radio station, and new personnel, or perhaps to see to the labour relations, to see how they would be hired. So it was probably it, but I cannot really vouch that that was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next says "convoy organisation." Do you know what that refers to? Under that, Djuro Bulic, the MUP of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a convoy that was to be organised to take some merchandise to Serbia and bring some other merchandise from there. It was at the time when the corridor to Serbia through Posavina was opened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you were receiving from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbia, we were mostly buying foodstuffs that were in short supply, that is, all flour, edible oil, all of the quantities needed. There was spices, fuel was also coming from there, but it wasn't the first-hand supply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... whether from Serbia were being received supplies and equipment relating to the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar as they were supposed to guard it, that is, the police was to guard it against possible theft or plunder, and the army was to provide escort through the areas where there were still combats going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Do you know from your own knowledge whether the army and/or the police were obtaining equipment and materiel from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. For the major part of the war, we had old uniforms, and I know that ways and means were sought to pay to some textile factories to somehow come by new uniform, because the old were already worn and torn. Because in Bosanski Petrovac, I think that there were these remains of the army even in 1995, when we left. Those were huge stocks for a war that could last many years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just concentrate on 1992? If you don't know the answer, say so straight away, Judge. But do you know whether or not Serbia was supplying equipment to either the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no direct knowledge of that, but my impression is that it was quite possible, because people came from there or went there. But military commands would know more about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, one moment, if I may interrupt you. Please forgive me if I am interrupting you. But I would like to know whether there is any connection at all between the first part of this entry and the second part of this entry. You have convoy organisation, Djuro Bulic, MUP of Krajina, with his telephone number, and then there is intelligence centre, with the telephone number of the MUP of the ARK, Autonomous Region, and also reference to Nikola Erceg with also his telephone number. Is there a relation between, connection between the organisation of this convoy and the intelligence unit of the MUP of the ARK, and Nikola -- and the president of the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is. It is all connected, because this is one note. One had to organise the convoy, and the merchandise which was already ready for the market had to be loaded. Then the number of vehicles and their registration numbers had to be supplied to the police, and this is the number of the contact. And also to inform the ARK government that our convoy would be on its way so that they could lend it support when it goes to their region. So it's all related.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And my apologies, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we've dealt with that, but can we just go over to the other side of the page under the 3rd of July. A request to Milorad Sajic for the delivery of cigarettes and you've written in brackets member of the Crisis Staff of the ARK. Do you remember why Mr. Sajic, or as he was, in fact, Lieutenant Colonel Sajic, had anything to do with cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cigarettes were in a very short supply at the time, and it was very difficult to procure them. The stocks in the Banja Luka factory were very small and insufficient. The pre-war reserves had already been spent and there was a major pressure coming from the army to provide with cigarettes. And that is why we communicated with the Crisis Staff and asked them to help us find some connections so that we could buy them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know why it was Lieutenant Colonel Sajic in particular that you were contacting? If you don't, say so, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Late President Novakovic always gave me such numbers at the time and told me who to communicate with and what to ask for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. We can move then, please, in your diary still, to the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's page 138, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that day, did you go to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to these notes, it was either that day or perhaps a few days later. These notes just are a list of things I have to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of the first things we see is that you were going to see Rosic about Svabo. Was that Rosic, the judge?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic was a judge. At that time, he held a high office in the judiciary, and the president had told me to talk with him in relation to Svabo. Svabo is that Nikola Kovacevic's nickname. He was another judge. So he told me to speak with Rosic and the president told me literally to ask him whether Svabo was a suitable person for the office of a judge, because at that time the court was being set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Rosic was in charge, was he, of appointments of judges for the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Petrovac court?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the assembly which appointed judges. But we simply didn't know those people enough, and people who work in the judiciary usually know one another. So all we needed was some information whether that man would be good for the job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, then if we go down that note, we see, it states: "To drop in to the Crisis Staff at 1100 hours." And if you go, then, to the next page, you've headed it "The meeting of the War Presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." And you were shown this in interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is at page 83 of the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the one and only time that you actually attended a meeting of the War Presidency of the Autonomous Region?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I attended it only once, and I've already told you that it was my impression that it had not been prepared properly. But on that day, I must have been present. And it is also quite possible that I was present on two occasions, once that there was a specific reason for me to go there, that I went there with a specific purpose in mind, and on another occasion I just happened to be doing something else in the vicinity. But it seems that I was present at that meeting that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps I can deal with this by reminding you what you said in your interview so we can deal with it fairly quickly. Did you in fact, when you put down analyse, number 1, analyse implementation of the previously adopted measures and decisions, and you were asked whether that was the regional Crisis Staff or War Presidency, analysing the implementation of its decisions by the municipalities. And your answer was: "Probably. Most probably, because I don't see what other decisions there would be." Do you still think that was right when you said that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, absolutely, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the report on the shortage and surplus of strategic products in the Autonomous Region. I think that's fairly clear. Then a report by the agency on the moving of material goods and people. I don't know whether you remember. Do you remember what that agency was, or what that agency was called?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite recall. Many bodies were established. And then they did only one or two tasks, and formally there were never disassembled and there were many bodies that were set up ad hoc. But bearing in mind this report on moving material goods and people, it says here that a thousand people -- I can't see any further. It is possible -- it is possible that this refers to either the movement of the population that had arrived in our region, because this used to be called -- this settlement used to be called a colony, kolonija, and there were many buildings still left which could have been adapted for accommodation of population. Several hundreds of people used to live in this place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As I say, I don't want to spend too long on this, because we've still got a little bit to get through. We see conclusions. One reporter, it says, for Petrovac Krupa, and is that Bihac? Can you just tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that a conclusion is that one report from the session should be sent to the relevant organs of these municipalities, for their deliberation. Because further on in this report there is also a remark where the borders are, which means that it is for these municipalities, it was asked up to which border should the army hold the positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then composition. Members of the SDS regional board, deputies, and members of the ARK or Presidency. Was that the composition of the meeting you were -- attended or does it refer to something else?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That was not the composition of the meeting. It is obvious that here it is about who will be the member or who will be sending this report, which means that this should have been held certainly before the BH assembly, so that then this should be discussed in a joint assembly. That was one thing. The second thing was that in this body, this body should include members of the SDS regional boards, deputies, and members of the War Presidency of the ARK. So this composition should have worked out the proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, finally, as to who was at this meeting, who was presiding in the meeting that you attended?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The session that I attended, I remember well that it was Mr. Brdjanin that chaired the session. I don't know whether it was this session or it was a session that, as far as I recall, took place earlier in the year. But before the war clashes started in Krajina, in general. I know that on one occasion I went, either it was in the assembly of Banja Luka assembly, whether it was in their building, I'm not certain. At one session that I attended, Mr. Brdjanin chaired the session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you remember, and was there anybody else there that you recognised, first of all, from the regional Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure individually. It is possible that Mr. Kupresanin attended. I didn't know these people. I arrived in this region just before the war started, and I had heard about most of the people. I personally knew from Banja Luka, I knew Dr. Lukic, as far as politicians are concerned, I also knew another one, a director of a rubber industry. These were presidents of the SDS. They were all replaced. I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said -- or it was translated Dr. Lukic. Did you mean Dr. Vukic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukic. Vukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's all that I need to ask you about that. Now, I want to move in a moment to the way in which the Muslims left Bosanski Petrovac. But before that, I'd like you to have a look at a document, please, that was produced by someone else, and that is Exhibit 1878, which you were given a chance to look at last week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, that's referred to in his statement, at page 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this was not a document written by you or that you had seen before, but did you have an opportunity to read through it when the investigator showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity, and I read it carefully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, is this an accurate account of events as it affected the Muslims in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a -- an accurate account of events. It's possible that certain details are not quite accurate, but not deliberately, but simply because they didn't know the facts. But yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you yourself were aware, for example, of the incident which happened on the 18th of June, where two people were killed by a bomb being thrown into their bedroom, and I think, in fact, you described it to us.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the house of these people was located in the neighbourhood that I lived in. In the morning when I set off for work, I saw police, and I saw that they were conducting an on-site investigation. And when I came to work, I asked what happened, and I was told that a grenade had been thrown through the window of the bedroom where these people had been sleeping in at the time. These were elderly people, or rather, they were 50 to 60 years old. And they died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, under the incident for July 14th, we see the reference to two mosques being blown up. Were all the mosques in Bosanski Petrovac either destroyed or damaged, that is, in the municipality itself?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Petrovac, as far as I know, there were three mosques. All three of them were in the town area, or rather, the wider area of town, and all three of them were destroyed. They were not just damaged; they were completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then if we go, please, to the page -- the following page, we see a reference to meetings between the Muslims, Mr. Novakovic, and then UNPROFOR. And I want to deal with those, because you recorded them in your diary. Could you turn, please, first of all, to the -- I'm sorry. Before we get to that, can you look in your diary at the 10th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's at page 150. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talk about the Balic family being liquidated by Muslim extremists. This is a press release, apparently. And then the propaganda is under way to expel all Muslims, which is unacceptable. First of all, where was the Balic family?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the president's instructions, I was the person in charge of the contact with the media, generally speaking. And I was in charge of conducting these tasks in relation to the movements and departures. As far as Balic family is concerned, this is to do with the Biscani incident. It is always referred to as an incident. The murder of this family really struck the rating of the leadership. This is the family which never in any way expressed disloyalty to the authority. These were people, citizens, who did not express their animosity or suspicions. Balic was a well-to-do man, and the chief of police, in secret, so people wouldn't know, although this can be found in the documents, had given him a Kalashnikov to defend his property, because there was a danger that he would be attacked because of his wealth. But in spite of that, somebody went into his house in a peaceful way and killed his family and him. And it was never established who had done that. This incident has been referred to time and time again, because it influenced a great deal the decisions of the leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- I'm sorry. Do I understand this: You were told to arrange for a press release to say that the Balic family had been liquidated by Muslim extremists, even though that wasn't the case, or you didn't -- or the policemen didn't know that to be the case?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To start with, in the initial information, the police suspected that some of the Muslims might have done that, because Mr. Balic publicly stated that he had nothing against Serbs, Serb army, et cetera, and he had even bought a large bull and given it as a present to one of the representatives of the command to be used for -- by the army as food. And that was the first. But it was not found out. It was not known at the time who had killed him. There were only suspicions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then the propaganda is under way to expel all Muslims, which is unacceptable. From whom was the propaganda coming?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall who this referred to, but the propaganda in this direction came from certain of their representatives, perhaps because people were scared, which was to be expected in these circumstances. But probably it came from other sides possibly as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you -- is what you're saying, it came from them, that the Muslims themselves were putting up propaganda to expel all of their own nationality?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, the expression propaganda, in my opinion, is too strong a word. As far as I recall, this was not about propaganda. It was about the fact that people spoke to each other and came to the conclusion that under these circumstances, they should move out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is the word that you used in your diary "expel"?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. To move out. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you read out, please, so we can get a translation, the exact words that you wrote underneath the word -- the sentence underneath the Balic family.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Propaganda is under way for all the Muslims to move out, which is unacceptable."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Who was saying that all the Muslims should move out, which you were writing down as unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about a language barrier. This note is a crude observation, a crude note. These are instructions that I had been given by the president so that I would work them over and then pass them on to the press. But what it means is that for the press, what I should say, that there is propaganda under way, obviously, not specifying who it was coming from, that all the Muslims -- for all the Muslims to move out and that this propaganda was unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not that difficult a question, Judge. Was it the Muslims who were putting out this propaganda, in inverted commas, that they should move out, or was it Serbs putting out propaganda that all Muslims should be moved out?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, that's precisely the problem. What the idea was, it was to tell the press that the Muslims themselves were authors of this propaganda, with the objective of them moving out, or rather, some of their representatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that true, that the Muslims themselves were putting out the propaganda that they should move out?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was -- is that they were not carrying on with this propaganda, but because of the circumstances, they were asking for shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we move in your diary, please, to a couple of the meetings with the internationals. 13th of August, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 153 for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend a meeting at UNPROFOR with what looks like a French captain, Philippe Lavergne and then Mr. Odobasic, Mr. Druzic. Can you remember, please, what the first name of Mr. Druzic was?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Odobasic is concerned, I know he's Husein, but as far as Druzic is concerned, I can't recall at this moment. But I believe he only had one leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The chief of the SJB, was that Mr. Gacesa?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Odobasic was explaining the problems which we needn't go through, ending up with remaining in Petrovac is a catastrophe for us. And then if we go, please, to the 17th of August in your diary, page 156, was there a meeting on the 17th of August with UNHCR and some military observers? Was it clear that UNHCR was saying they will not participate in the resettlement of population?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This is an accurate transcription of their opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And can we just go, please, to the 21st of August, and then I'm going to go to the other documents that relate to the movement out. On the 20th of August, you're making some notes, and I think -- is this a reference to the letter we saw on -- I'm sorry - on the 21st of August, reply to the SIP, which is the letter we looked at -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recall that letter. I wrote it personally. And I was given the instructions to do that by the president of the Executive Board. This is a letter which talks about -- it's a response regarding the decision to sack Muslims from the firm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was P2452.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, now can we look, please, at what happened in September. First of all, can you have a look at Exhibit 1848. And that's apparently a news item put out by Mr. Dosen, who you spoke about earlier, which is dated the 13th of September. The mass departure of Muslims from the area of Bosanski Petrovac is handwritten -- sorry, still continuing. A column of seven buses with a special escort departed from the village of Biscani in the direction of Travnik. According to information from the Petrovac office for the exchange of population and property over the last three days, more than 900 men, women, and children of Muslim ethnicity have moved from the area of Petrovac. According to Serbian and municipality War Presidency sources, the departure of the Petrovac Muslims can in no way be compared with ethnic cleansing. Not a single Muslim from this area has left under pressure but of their own free will. Now, you dealt with this in the statement that you made last week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is at page 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, the expression "not a single Muslim from this area has left under pressure but of its own free will," was that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's have a look, please, at what happened on the 13th of September, because you were intimately concerned with those events. Can you look, please, at P1849. You had a chance to read through that document, again when you made the statement, and if you look at the second page, there's a description of what happened when you arrived. This was a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. report -- I think it should be not Sacesa but Gacesa who wrote that report. Is that an accurate report of what happened on that convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who tried to leave that day, were they able to leave?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not able to leave because there were combat operations along the route that they were supposed to travel on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was it that caused you to start this argument with the police?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the impossibility -- due to the impossibility that our convoy was to pass, we were informed about this five to six hours before I managed to get to Karanovac. President Novakovic on that day was in Lika somewhere. He was escorting our church delegation or something like that. And I managed to get in touch with him on the phone, and he said that by hook or by crook I should go there, get them out, and certainly, with the assistance of the president in the municipality over there, Knezevo, protect them and once the combat operations died down on the front, that they should then cross. When I got there, I found the police and those buses with the refugees in Karanovac. It's a place near Banja Luka. Around the buses, there were various men, some in uniform, some in part uniform, some without uniform. They were armed, mostly with older army weapons. But there were quite a few automatic weapons. I saw that the buses were surrounded. Police were standing aside and they were speaking to some people who were not armed. Immediately I headed for the buses to see whether there was -- if there was anyone who was killed or wounded. And I went through the buses, and I was being cursed by those people who were standing by the buses. I mean, they were cursing my everything. It's useless for me to actually quote them. Literally, it's just the worst things I've heard. But they said that I was defending, protector of Muslims, traitor and what not, and that I was very bitter. I did tell them that they should be ashamed of themselves, that if they wanted to fight, they should go to the front rather than terrorise unarmed people, civilians. And once I went through the buses, I knew a few men among the Muslims, and I know that I spoke briefly with our head of accounting, Senada, and she looked at me. Her eyes were full of tears. She had two small children with her and she said: Jovo, are you going to kill us all here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's what led to the argument that's described?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the 13th of September. Now could you have a new document, please, and that is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's got the number 7.283 on it, Your Honour, something that he -- a new document, something that he brought with him. It's dated the 23rd of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, of these notes you made, apparently, it looks like on the back of a restaurant bill, of a meeting on the 23rd of September of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The bill had nothing to do with this. It just happened to be there. But it was done in a small notebook. We just -- we just there happened to be in the office. And that evening when they summoned me to a meeting, it was an urgent, ad hoc meeting of the War Presidency which had to do with the transfer of the population, relocation of the population, after the violence escalated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And can we just summarise the escalation, the violence, because we've heard about it before, and you spoke about it at the interview. Some Serbs had been killed on the front line by some Muslims, and as a result, were Serbs in Petrovac taking revenge on the Muslims in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had this urgent meeting on the 23rd of September at just before midnight, 2345. Present, Mr. Novakovic. Was that Mr. Gacesa as chief?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bogdan --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogdan -- shall I give you the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Give us all the names, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: So Rajko Novakovic, the president; chief of the police, Dragan Gacesa; Bogdan Latinovic, president of the Executive Board; Jevto Kecman, police commander; Nenad Dragisic, chief of the military security in Petrovac; and Drago Sepa, he's the father of Jovica Sepa who was in the TO command, the TO units which are local units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the meeting was about the security situation, and Mr. Novakovic apparently condemned the killing of innocent civilians and said he would submit his resignation unless the authorised organs prevent the pogrom, and believes it is not accidental, et cetera. Do you know what he meant by using the words "believes it is not accidental"?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that together with the police and other competent agencies, Mr. Novakovic and the rest of us tried to do something. That is, Mr. Novakovic requested that some people be arrested, and some of them were. But in the very early days of that campaign, their friends and allies abducted them from the police, and before that, Mr. Novakovic was saying that he might resign. But he said that privately, in a narrow circle. However, he thought that then the situation would only get worse. I believe that his appraisal was right. He was quite an influential figure and he could keep things under control. And this is when he says this in public. What the gist of this is is that he believed that these were organised groups, because he knew those people before the war, I mean those who were engaged in violence, and he knew what they could do. So presumably that was why he thought that they were not acting quite on their own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Organised by whom? Did he know that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, at that time, and now, I think that he was making some guesses. He had some hypotheses as to who could be behind those people. But he never told me that, and in the war he was killed on our side, on the Serb side, under pretty vague circumstances. But he never said anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I don't think, other than to note that if we look at -- for our page 6 of the translation, at one point the chief says: All services had indications as to who are the perpetrators. And then the president states: Arranging a meeting for tomorrow morning, and if order is not established, the entire civilian leadership shall submit their resignations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honours, there's various discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was the upshot of all of this that arrangements were made to get buses -- you were ordered to arrange for buses to effectively transport all the Muslims out of Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the chief of the police saying that the police had some indicias as to who could be the perpetrators of this violence. And again, the chief of the military security does not contest that, and says that his service will see to it that all the army members, that is, uniformed men, bearing weapons, be removed from the town, in order to eliminate the danger threatening those who -- to the convoy. And my task was then to tell all the firms and companies, and especially hauliers transporting companies, all those who could provide us with a means of transportation, that they should set off early in the morning with full guards to the places -- to the meeting points and to also provide some security on the way and to head towards Travnik. And I talked with the transport companies. Some complied with the agreement and provided the vehicles, others didn't, but the convoy left on the 24th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, I think, again, if I can deal with this fairly quickly, you told us in interview - this is page 87, Your Honours - that somebody proposed that their money and jewellery be taken from them, but you objected, saying that it was illegal. And that was accepted. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The suggestion was, and it came mostly from the military command. I think it was Mr. Vrzina who presented the views of the troops on the front line. He did not attend this meeting, because it was an emergency meeting, so he simply couldn't make it. Of course, others disagreed with this, but they kept silent, because it would have been embarrassing for them to refuse their proposal. They knew it was nonsense. But since he was not present at the meeting, it was not discussed at all. And technically, it was unfeasible, not to mention that it was unlawful, and everybody understood that. And he was trying to say that they would use that money to buy the weapons and then wage war against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think you accompanied that convoy.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: True, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think it's also right that there was, in fact, an attack on the convoy.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. There was an attack on the convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And some people were killed, and others wounded.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, what I learnt during the escort, four people were killed and eight sustained wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Finally, Judge, can I just ask you, please, to look at a couple more exhibits that are in the binder. First of all, P1850.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not on my list, but it deals with this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we do that, Ms. Korner, are you tendering this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Can I exhibit that document, please, which will be P2453.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the minutes of the 22nd of -- 23rd of September. I'll just confirm, that has the disclosure number 7.283.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a public announcement made, apparently -- is it signed again by Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was -- it was a public announcement to be made. Was that in connection with the killings that were going on which he was trying to stop?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to do with the murders which happened after the soldiers were killed on the front, wanton killing of Muslims started, as it is indicated in that other document, and that is why he tried to make this announcement, to do something about it, that is, to stop that. And that is, he talks about the knightly traditions and also calls upon people not to waste ammunition. But this is again for propaganda purposes, so Serbs would accept it, to understand that even from that particular point of view it would do damage. Because it was largely firing without any particular target. But also shots were fired to kill people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can put that away. Now can you have, finally, documents 1852, 1853, 1854, and 1855, 1856, and 1857. That's it. Well, actually, you had better have 8 -- the whole lot, Your Honour. It's just one small point but I'm just going to get this all done. 1858 and 1859.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And again, Judge, while you look at these documents, if you have reason to doubt the authenticity of any them, please draw our attention to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I think that something is not authentic, yes, I will tell you so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the point is this and then you can just confirm it because you have already dealt with it. After the assembly had met and verified the decisions, were all those decisions reissued in October -- on October the 28th? Because they all, in fact, are copies of earlier decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours may recall that when the witness was here, it wasn't clear why all these decisions were being made.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already spoken about organisational inconsistency. The names of the Crisis Staff and War Presidency were often interchanged, or the presidency of the assembly, or whatever. I worked for those agencies, but I really don't know what they were called, because they kept changing them. This document that I'm looking at is the decision on the appointment of the Crisis Staff, as a document where such matters were cleared up. Most of the people listed here are there ex officio and because of the offices and jobs that they held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do not worry about that. If you look at the dates on all these documents, they're all the same date, the 28th of October, by which time, as you've explained to us, there was hardly a Muslim left in Petrovac. All I'm trying to establish, particularly if you look at P1857, the date at the top is the 18th of June. It refers to a meeting of the Crisis Staff on the 17th of June and then a date has been added, the 28th of October. Was this simply a formality, to reissue the decisions that had been taken after their verification by the assembly?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see. The two decisions that I'm looking at on the 28th of October 1992, now I know why they were taken. All these decisions of the Crisis Staff, or the War Presidency, had to be under the then regulations, had to be submitted to the assembly of the municipality for verification. And these are working papers prepared for the councilmen. So that regardless of when the decisions were taken, they had to be submitted to the assembly for verification, and that is why they were done in this sequence and in a series.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Judge. That's all that I want to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, going back, returning to what we discussed in the beginning of the sitting, any further documents that you would like the witness to authenticate?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. What I'm going to do is when he's finished being cross-examined, I'm going to ask him to make a further -- to go through all the documents that he hasn't been shown and ask him to authenticate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you have any objection to that, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Perfect. Do you want to start now or shall we have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If we could have the break now, I'd appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you would agree to that. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry about the delay. Mr. Cunningham. Judge, you're going to be cross-examined by Mr. Cunningham now, who is appearing for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Cunningham:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I know, obviously, you are a lawyer, and at least where I come from, lawyers tend to be long-winded and talk a lot. I know it's your wish to be home with your family as soon as possible, and it's my goal to get that accomplished as soon as possible. So before we start, I want to remind you of several things. First of all, when you started testifying last Thursday, the President of this Chamber asked you to answer the questions that I ask you, or any other lawyer asks you, as precisely as you can, so I'd like for you to do that. Secondly, if you do not understand my question, please let me know. The third thing I'm going to ask is: I know that you have looked over your tape-recorded statement that you gave to the OTP in June of 2003, but I'd ask that, out of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. fairness to you, that you be provided with a copy of your statement, your tape-recorded statement, as well as the statement you gave last week, so that you can look at them if the need arises. So I'd ask that he be provided with a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar. These two statements, or rather, the statement plus the transcript of the interview, are to be handed or to be made available to the witness straight away. I suppose that's the B/C/S version that you gave him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And if at any time you need to refer to your notes, either be they your diary, the interview with the OTP, please do so and take as much time as you need to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Cunningham, if I may interrupt you, I think it's wise to have also the photocopy of his diary available.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think he has it right in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think what he has there is the diary -- he has already. Okay. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, sir, when I talk about an exhibit, I will do my best to get that exhibit in front of you so that you can review it so that we can talk about the exhibit and communicate properly. I'm going to start now, and I understand that the Office of the Prosecutor no longer considers you to be a suspect, but when you were in that tape-recorded interview in June of 2003, and you were warned that you were a suspect, what thoughts came to your mind when you heard that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can frankly say that I was surprised. I was concerned, and I was wondering what the reasons for that would be. I carried out different tasks. I was at different posts, as secretary of the Executive Board. Later on I was a judge. While doing these jobs, I had necessarily done certain things that some people may not have liked. Also, I was in conflict with certain representatives of the command and the police, as you were able to see from the documents, and I thought that it could have been somebody's report, information, but I kept going over it in my mind, and I couldn't quite work out what that would be, and I was simply worried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Worried because, in your mind, I take it, you feel that you had done nothing wrong?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was worried as to how to prove that I haven't done things. At the time, I did not know that there were certain documents also that had been presented here, and I didn't know people very well in that region, and I was simply wondering who I could propose as a witness to confirm that I hadn't done anything that would be considered as illegal or against the rules. Here, there was no discussion. On one or more occasions I was a negotiator trying to help the Muslims to provide protection for them, and I was going to propose one of them as a witness for me, but I didn't know their names. So I wasn't afraid because of what I may have possibly done, but I was worried that I wouldn't be able to prove that I hadn't done anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then came to The Hague, and I don't recall if you were in Court when it was announced to this Chamber that you were no longer considered a suspect. Did the Office of the Prosecutor tell you why they had changed their status, that is, at first you were a suspect and then you were not considered a suspect? Did they give you a reason why?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that they had studied the case more carefully, that they had studied the documents, and that they believed, according to their new information, had no reason to suspect me, and that they would only be questioning me as a witness. I was told that by Mr. -- Mr. -- I'm sorry. That was Mr. Grady who had told me this. I have to stress that here I have a version in English of the transcript, so if it is necessary for me to follow, I would need to have a version in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. That's what I thought too, and that's why I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for pointing that out. It was my suspicion from the beginning, and that's why I said it needs to be in B/C/S. So the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a clean copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a clean copy too. I mean, so let's -- the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- has one as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript of your interview, is that -- Judge, let's go through what you have over there. You have a copy of your diary, or your notebook, and that, I suppose, is in its original, in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also have a copy of the interview, the long interview, in other words. Is it in English or in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to replace that with the B/C/S. That's the thick -- the 80 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The registry only provide with the English transcript. We don't have the statement here. We have never been provided with the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can provide the witness with my own, so let's not waste time. I don't understand why the Registry shouldn't have one, while I, who doesn't read the language, should have one. But anyway --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. That's what I just said. It's I would say highly unlikely that we would give to Your Honours something that we don't give to the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I can't -- where I can't help is with the then statement of the 22nd and 23rd of July. I have it -- I have two copies of that, but they're both in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I have a ready, clean copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If you can assist us there, Mr. Cunningham, please make it available to the witness, who will then return it back at the end of his testimony. All right. I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we had our short break dealing with these exhibits, I had -- you had told us how you were informed by Mr. Grady that you were no longer considered a suspect. My next question is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I hate to interrupt. It's right to say, so Mr. Cunningham knows, he was informed of this by me with Mr. Grady present and a full note was taken of what I said by Mr. Grady and I think -- but I think Mr. Cunningham deserves to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, sir, is simply this: Once you were informed by the OTP, how did that make you feel, that you were no longer a suspect?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be frank, I didn't feel anything in particular, because I believe that there would be no grounds for any charges and that there would never be any. While I started giving my statement and when Ms. Korner came and told me that, this was mentioned almost in passing with Mr. Grady there. For me, nothing had changed. It was only later that I started thinking about it, and I thought: Well, they had really suspected me seriously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when they told you you were no longer considered a suspect, did you feel any sense of relief whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time, or later. Simply, I know what had been going on, and I know what I did at the time, what I undertook, and not just myself; there's only a part of that in the documents, and only one part is encompassed in the statement because it's simply impossible to have all that in one case. But I knew that there couldn't be any well-founded charges. So I simply accepted this as something that was said in passing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, the tape-recorded statement, and our page numbers may be off between the English version and the Serbo-Croatian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. version, but on page 4 of the English version, you make the following statement, and on the English version it's on lines 9 and 10 of page 4: "I remember quite a lot, but then again, memory can be deceiving, and I'd like to tell you why I believe that." Now, obviously, here you're talking about, in that passage, you're talking about how you had to flee Petrovac, but that statement causes some concern on my part, because you're saying in this statement that at times your memory may deceive you. How can you allay my concerns and those concerns of my client that your memory is intact?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the nature of things, it is impossible for memory to be complete. I made a solemn declaration before this Court that I would be telling the truth, and I know that this is my duty. Certainly, memory can be deceptive, but this statement, this initial part of the statement, I made until -- or rather, before my minutes and records, diaries were presented to me, and I have to frankly say that I would have had trouble remembering a lot of what I had stated if I hadn't seen these notes and diaries, particularly the names and the functions. Certainly some tasks. You were able to see for yourself, for instance, that the so-called incident in Biscani, it is only before the Court that I remembered what this was about. Throughout this time, I had thought that this was about a completely different location. I wasn't sure what had gone on. But it was only later that I realised that it was the murder of that family, of that businessman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I appreciate and understand and respect the fact that looking at your notes and other documents, your memory has been refreshed, and some things become clearer to you now, but I would ask you if you're not sure of an answer, would you please tell us so, or if you're not sure of specific events, please tell us so. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to start my substantive questioning with you by looking at a passage at page 91 of the English transcript, and it's at line -- starts at line 14. And to put this in the proper context for you, sir, this question, this passage, comes up near the end of your interview, when you're asked by Ms. Korner and her assistants if you would be willing to appear before this Tribunal voluntarily, and you agree to do that, and you give your reasons. And I want to read you one of the reasons and I'm going to quote what you said. This starts actually at line 13: "Because of the general situation and -- was going on, I believe that the municipal authorities there did whatever was possible. The essential goal, the essential intention, was for people to be removed from danger, and unfortunately, if you look at it from the outside, we seem exactly the same, in a way, as the municipalities that organised the persecution of their population and organised their removal." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. I remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wonder, and I'd like to ask you if you agree with this proposition, that things may not always appear -- things may not always be what they appear to be; that is, while it may appear that your municipality and people like you involved in that municipal government were involved in cleansing and persecution, it really was not that way. Do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To claim that the situation in Petrovac was not like in other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think my question really was this: Judging by what you said at page 91 of your interview, that is, "if you look at it from the outside, we seem exactly the same, in a way, as the municipalities that organise the persecution of the population and organise their removal," if you look at that passage, it seems to me what you're saying is some people might draw that conclusion that Petrovac was involved in persecution, in organised removal for cleansing purposes, but that really wasn't the case in Petrovac. I want to see if you'll agree with that proposition.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. It wasn't like that. The situation wasn't like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You -- although you -- I'm going to ask you some questions now about your background, and taking the job in Petrovac. Although you were born in the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac, you were largely raised and educated in other municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly in the municipality of Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have told us in your statement and in your testimony that you were, in effect, in 1990, 1991, when you came to Petrovac, you were new to the municipality, that you really did not know a lot of individuals in that municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was, for all intents and purposes, a new municipality for you, with very few contacts within the municipality itself?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to your training, obviously you're a lawyer and you've told us about your training in administrative matters, having received a degree from the higher administrative school in Zagreb, and that's correct; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you received your law degree, you remained in Zagreb, where you were working at a Croatian school; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was there, I guess in 1990, where you learned and experienced first-hand interethnic conflict when you had to leave that school because of the hostilities directed towards you, a Serb, from the Croats at that school; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the assistance of some friends, you received a job offer from the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that offer came from the president, Mr. Novakovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it from reading your statements, hearing your testimony, that you admired and respected Mr. Novakovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I respected him, but I didn't admire him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Getting back to -- coming to the municipality, in your English statement, in your tape-recorded statement in the English translation, is what I should say, near the bottom of page 7, in talking about going to this new job with the municipality, you stated, on line 29: "It was not your intention at all to go there." Could you explain to me what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that on that occasion. I was an active member of the orthodox community in Zagreb, religious community, and a large number of younger people gathered there. And when I had suffered verbal attacks for being a Serb, I confided in some of them from the community, and some of them who were in good relations with the bishop, a group of us spoke about it. It is the metropolitan from Zagreb himself said to me that he would be able to ensure a job for me in Belgrade. Although I had thought about staying in Zagreb further on. I didn't want to accept the Belgrade option, because it was an environment that I wasn't used to. And when I went to see my parents, it was the holidays. I met some friends from school and we spoke a while about all this, about me thinking about leaving Zagreb or not. And one of them had spoken - I don't know who exactly. Perhaps several of them had spoken to this president who was a director of a company at the time - and when I returned to Zagreb, we agreed that we would meet for a drink. So I stopped by a cafe. But on that occasion, this Mr. Novakovic, who at the time was not the president, they introduced me to him and he started talking me into coming to Petrovac. I didn't agree then. He was saying that after the elections, most probably his party would be the first and that he would be able to ensure a position for me. However, I didn't accept. I said I didn't know what I would do, and so on. It didn't please me to go to an environment that I didn't know. A small environment, and that I wouldn't be able to find many Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. things in that I had been used to. After that, Mr. Novakovic called me on several occasions. He called me while I was in Zagreb, when I was there, and when I wasn't there. And on a couple of occasions a friend of mine in Zagreb, Ivica Bezer, received these calls and told me I should return these calls because Mr. Novakovic was very persistent. And at that time it became quite probable that he would become the president, because the elections, I think, may have already passed. And finally, because of his persistence, I returned his call. And again, I didn't accept, and it was only on the third or fourth occasion when we spoke I said I would go and see. And then in December 1990 I went there and he then introduced a large group of assemblymen, and said we had several positions for lawyers and that I should say myself what would suit me most and suit my qualifications and my wishes. At that time, the secretary of the assembly hadn't been named, or of the municipal board. I don't know, chiefs of various services. And I thought that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you have answered my question as to what your intent was, and it sounds like, to me, that Mr. -- your president, Mr. Novakovic, ultimately convinced you to join the municipality and that you did so. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were officially appointed as secretary of the executive committee; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, at times you performed the function of the secretary to the Municipal Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You certainly had the experience and training in administrative matters to do that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also lived very, very close to the municipal building, so you were there readily available if they needed you; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I also get the impression that you're the sort of individual that will help out if asked. Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it is not too difficult or impossible, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And another reason why you, I take it, got involved with being the secretary for the Municipal Assembly is that your colleague, Mr. Sikman, was not really a hard worker, and you just assumed many of his responsibilities; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that is correct too. As a matter of fact, he was involved in other things beyond that office. One cannot say that he did not work, but he did not work there enough to be able to do everything. Even because he continued performing the tasks that he used to perform in the company for which he worked earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also, in addition to having these two tasks, being the secretary -- at times the secretary to the Municipal Assembly, the secretary to the executive committee, later on in your tenure at Bosanski Petrovac, you also served on the Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Formally at times I was appointed to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we'll get to your time with the Crisis Staff. Let's -- let me stay focused and talk to you about your early tenure at Petrovac. Now, I know from reading your transcripts and hearing your testimony, that there was a time that you were actually mobilised and called to the front lines. Do you remember the effective dates of your mobilisation, the days that you were in the military during this time period?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can give you some dates, but I can't really say that it is quite accurate. So the first time I was called up in early -- the first third -- no, was it March or April? I think it was March 1992. And I was called up to join the engineering regiment, as a lawyer. However --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... remember just to confine your call-ups to the time period of 1991 through 1992. Were there any more call-ups or mobilisations in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I stayed one month on the front, and then in 1992 I was mobilised on three more occasions. Once I was on Kupres, and twice on the Bihac front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand you cannot remember the specific dates, and I'm not asking you to. But during these four mobilisations that you had in 1992, roughly speaking, how long were you in the military?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All together -- all in all, between two and a half and three months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how much of that two and a half and three months were you away from Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's as long as I spent outside Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's safe to say during the time period that you were mobilised, that you were not tending to your obligations with the municipality because you had your obligations with the military?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be correct, by and large.
